utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. We are sitting today on a Friday. That was pursuant to the request of the accused not to sit the Monday of this week to enable him to participate in a religious celebration in the Detention Unit. I just wanted to put this on the record. Before we continue the examination of the current witness, I would like to raise a specific matter. Last week we had a very unfortunate situation in our courtroom which was discussed twice since then. I refer to the conduct of the Prosecutor during the hearing on the 16th of February. The Chamber finds itself in a very unsatisfactory situation. We, the Judges, considered the situation very seriously and the many aspects. This is the reason why we come back to the matter only today, which is very unfortunate. As the Presiding Judge of this Chamber, I would like to provide the participants of the trial with my personal view. As the Presiding Judge, it is my obligation to ensure a fair as well as an expeditious trial with full respects for the rights of the accused. I have to establish and maintain a good atmosphere in the courtroom and a cooperative and professional relation between the parties. Further, I have to guarantee the invaluable position of every single Judge of this Bench. The conduct of the Prosecutor in question raises two serious concerns which I addressed already earlier. We have to rely on the information about the availability of witnesses provided by either party. Neither the opposing party - in this case, the Defence - nor the Chamber should be put under unnecessary time pressure but incorrect information. Or to put it in other terms, we don't want to be misled. More serious were, in our view, the critical remarks of the Prosecutor with respect to questions and remarks of Judge Mindua. This was a totally unacceptable behaviour. Every Judge has the unlimited right to put questions to witnesses. No party has the permission for any criticism in this respect. It is very unfortunate that this has to be recalled in this courtroom. Mr. McCloskey, you know all of that. Even in very emotional moments in such a trial everybody has to bear that in mind. This is one precondition for our successful work. Mr. McCloskey, the Judges have taken notice of your repeated apologies. I refer to your immediate apology at the same hearing, you're apologies you conveyed through Mr. Vanderpuye the next day, and to your statement you gave on Tuesday this week. This statement, in my view, was very honest and impressive, and I take it word for word. On my part, I accept your apologies. I'm sure that you will agree with the statement of the Chamber of 17th February and with my guidance of today. You will bear that in mind during the remaining time of this trial. With respect to the need to re-establish good and trusting relations, we should now look into the future and make sure that nothing like this will happen again. This concludes the matter. The witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, good morning to everybody. Perhaps it will be good to mention before the witness is brought in that a year ago to this day we had a Pre-Trial Conference in this case, so it is, in fact, a year into the trial today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this reminder. I was not aware of that. But, indeed, it is a long trial and a very serious trial and we all have to do our very best to ensure that we will succeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Parsons. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you for allow -- and I want to thank you for allowing me to attend my religious ceremony and I'm sorry if I disrupted the schedule for that fact. I would like this trial to reflect God's will and not mine. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to the witness. As a follow-up to our yesterday's discussion, this is it my question: Does the independent [as interpreted] commission on missing persons in any way oversee the work of the federal commission's work with regard to missing persons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do not oversee it in a supervisory or official capacity. However, we do work alongside the commission at many grave-sites and assist them in the provision of technical assistance and scientific expertise with regard to the forensic excavation of the grave-sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Does this mean, in reference to the technical assistance and scientific expertise you give them, that the international commission has no obligation whatsoever to control the work of the federal commission in the process of gathering information and identifying missing persons and that it has no binding obligations in that regard whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, can the international commission issue any binding instructions or put a stop to any activity undertaken by the federal commission if it deems it necessary to do so?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we don't have authority in that -- in that manner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up Exhibit P1935 in e-court. This is from the Popovic case. 20880 is the transcript page, lines 22 through 25. We'd like Mr. Parsons to see what his testimony in that case was, and I'll be quoting it once we have it on our screens. Or perhaps I could start quoting it now because he'll able to respond from memory. "The International Commission for Missing Persons was routinely informed of the excavations" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Tolimir please repeat the last part of the quote because it was unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters ask you to repeat the last part of your quote because they didn't catch it. It is only records that you said: "The International Commission for Missing Persons was routinely informed of the excavations," and then it stopped. Please repeat the following part of the quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. President, I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, in my view, there is an urgent matter. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, it may very well be. I understand that what's big displayed in e-court is the under seal version of the transcript. What we should be displaying is the public version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this advice. That should be P1936. The same page, the same line. Thank you for your guidance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll repeat the entire sentence. I wanted the witness to see it because the transcript itself is quite unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So I'm quoting: "The International Commission for Missing Persons is very regularly involved in excavations." Below, it says that "the excavation of the grave-sites is not under the authority of the ICMP." This is my question: It follows from this that the excavation of the grave-sites is under the authority of the federal commission and that previously, up until 2000, it was under the authority of the ICTY OTP. My question is this: While excavations are ongoing, what is the party you receive information from on the excavations? And specifically from whom do you receive information about this grave-site's connection or lack thereof to the Srebrenica events? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a number of sources of information that are available to us. One would be information that we're aware of as a result of ICTY investigations. We also would obtain information from either the federal commission or currently the Missing Persons Institute, which is the national organisation that is responsible for the conduct in relation to missing persons cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was told by my Legal Assistant that the question was not properly interpreted in English, so I'll repeat it. What sort of information do you receive from the organisation involved in excavations or conducting excavations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in -- in so far as we work together in deploying to the site, very often some background information regarding what is known from any number of sources will be provided to the ICMP. But our conduct really is not dependant upon information that we have or do not have. It becomes an independent scientific investigation of that particular site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please give us a specific answer to this question because it hinges on many other questions. Please, what sort of information do you receive from the organisation exhuming graves? So that's what I'm interested. I'm only interested in the organisation which is exhuming grave-sites and not any other bodies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'll say that I myself do not often participate in the grave evacuations so I'm not a first-hand party to the transfer of information. But with regard to the provision of background information, I would say that that occurs in a relatively casual manner, to the extent that it does occur. In other words, there is not any formal reporting mechanism whereby information regarding the grave-site is formally transmitted to the ICMP, nor would there need to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, may I support Mr. Tolimir. I think it was a quite short and clear question. Which kind of information does your institution, your -- the ICMP, receive? What kind of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, formally it would be the location of the site and what is anticipated to be found there with regard to its size and therefore the technical resources that we would need to be deployed. Often that's not actually known precisely in advance of the evacuation because the information is not available prior to the exhumation. But the type of information that -- what might be provided is that it's -- it's thought to be related to the Srebrenica -- the fall of Srebrenica due to its proximity to other such, say, secondary mass graves. But honestly, I don't think that there is a lot of specific information that is frequently given to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons. In that case, can you tell us, did the ICMP take part in exhumations and does it take part in exhumations, and are you involved in the identification of persons who went missing in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We are very routinely involved in exhumations and we're very much involved in the identification of persons missing from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What do you mean when you say "routinely," if you can tell us, Mr. Parsons?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ICMP has either monitored or assisted in the physical recovery at over 3.000 grave-sites in Bosnia and a large number of those - I forget the number - that have come to be considered to be related to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll have to be happy with the answer as it stands, if you believe it is a matter of routine. Can you tell us, do you take part in exhumations and identification of individuals who went missing from Srebrenica or elsewhere in Bosnia in the course of 1992, 1993, and 1994? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We -- we were not involved in exhumations in those early periods. However, we have identified many people who went missing in those periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, in the course of the examination-in-chief, you said, at page 54, that around 23.000 persons are listed as missing in Bosnia. Do you provide any sort of services with a view to identifying these missing persons, since you are located in Bosnia, or do you only provide the information related to Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We are very much involved, quite equally involved, in the identification of all missing persons from Bosnia. The Srebrenica-related identifications are simply a representative subset of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons. In that case, can you please answer the following question: Are you involved in making matches between donor blood samples and bone samples of the victims gone missing in Srebrenica in 1992 through to 1994, or those who had gone missing in that same time-period generally in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would be involved in making those matches to anyone reported missing to us from any time-period relating to Srebrenica or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons. Does this mean that your information about a missing person from 1992 could be found and used in some statistical analyses compiled by the relevant state authority of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's be even more specific. Is it possible for, say, one of the sides to place the DNA findings which you found a match for as having been -- gone missing in 1992, 1993, or 1994 with the findings of those who went missing in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify what you mean by "sides"? I'm not aware of any ongoing conflict that has "sides" to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I meant the parties to the identification -- identification process. You, as the ICMP, are one party. There we have also the Bosnian commission. So when you send matches for victims who went missing in 1992 or 1993 or 1994, is it possible for, let's say, the Bosnian commission to list those victims among the victims gone missing in 1995? And would you have any responsibility to bear in that case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no Bosnia commission presently. This is a role that has been transitioned to a national unit called the Missing Persons Institute. But with that clarification, the sense of your question is clear, and the answer is, yes, that information could easily made available. And in fact, the ICMP regularly distributes to such stakeholders a full notification list of all identifications that have been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for stating in the transcript the exact name of the relevant Bosnian body which is the Missing Persons Institute. Can you also tell us, for the sake of the transcript, when the institute came into being exactly?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't be able to provide you with exact dates, and this isn't my area of -- of responsibility or specialisation. But I will tell you that, to my knowledge, the Missing Persons Institute was brought into existence by agreement in 2005, but implementation of its operational role has -- took until around 2008 to -- to become established.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can we now show Exhibit P193, again the transcript from the Popovic case, which we have on our screens. So we need page 23 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure about the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or, rather, yes it's what we have on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In answer to the Prosecutor's question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Tolimir please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we are on the wrong document. You quoted the wrong number. It is P1936. There was one number missing so that we have a wrong document on the screen. Back to the Popovic transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The page is 15 to 19 [Realtime transcript read in error "15219"]; page is 20873.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tolimir misspoke. When he is referring to "15 to 19," [Realtime transcript read in error "15219"] that were the lines, in my understanding, and not the page. Again, it is recorded incorrectly. I said "15 to," what means "through 19." Thank you very much for the correction. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am now going to quote what the gentleman said in response to the Prosecutor. The question was: "... how the location and place of disappearance is denoted in the ICMP database?" And you replied: "Well, I should mention that for individuals reported missing from anywhere in Bosnia regarding any event, the information that we get comes from the family members of the missing. So to associate it with Srebrenica, that would have been information that the family provided to us." So, if you can, would you please clarify what you meant by this, because it's a rather long answer, so could you explain to us the essence of all this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we collect reference blood samples from family members in order to identify their missing loved ones, they provide us with a certain amount of information that allows us to properly make use of that data. So we determine who the missing person is, what his relationship to the family members are, whether there's any additional missing persons that are also related to the -- the first missing person. And we inquire about the place and date of disappearance. And so it would from the family's information that would indicate that an individual was missing in relation to Srebrenica in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, please tell us whether the ICMP links the disappearance of a certain person to the fall of Srebrenica exclusively based on information provided by the family of that missing person to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In large part, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us whether the ICMP checks that information in any way and compares it with information that is it in the possession, for example, of the ICRC or the national Missing Persons Institute, as we now call it, the BH army, that also has lists of missing persons, et cetera. I mean whether you check the dates and the information that's in these lists.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We will make note, for example, if that missing person -- if the family informs us that the missing person is also on the ICRC list of missing. But, in fact, we do not have a comprehensive investigative programme that would seek to reconcile the various lists or to further investigate in any definitive fashion the nature of that missing person's report as it comes to us from the families.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you're under no obligation, I would like to ask a question regarding some practical matters. Are indications given to the ICMP by anyone if there is mismatch between the information that the ICMP has and information that -- that exists in other records, for example, information that the BH army has?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a difficult question to answer highly -- specifically. We -- we work very closely with many organisations and with families, et cetera, and so the ICMP's body of knowledge as a result of our interactions is very, very wide. So it's hard for me to be specific with regard to how our knowledge is updated or to what extent. However, let me say that, no, we -- for example, we do not cross-correlate with information from the BH army, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. In order to clarify the situation that arises, would you please look at document P1766. And this would be important to us because of the authority of your commission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] could we look at P17 -- P1776, page 97 in English. Could we please have it in e-court. It's a table from Mr. Brunborg's report which shows cases where there's a mismatch between the date of disappearance and the death of a person in the records of the Prosecution and the BH army. Now we don't have it on the screens yet. We can't see the table. We see page 1 of the report. There it is. Could we please turn it. Thank you. And could we zoom in so the witness could see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this -- this should not -- I think this should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The question is: Was the attention of the ICMP ever drawn to these inconsistencies that we can now see in this table number 6? Or was indication given to you about any other inconsistencies?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what inconsistencies you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at column number 4; vertical column number 4. Let's look at the first person. It says date of death 26 April 1992. That's how he's registered by the International Tribunal. Let's look at number 6 now, line 6, where it says that the date of death is 10 January 1994. And it says: "Location Buljim."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I touched the screen, and I ruined everything. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, it was not you, Mr. Tolimir. It was the witness. But that happens several times. You can't avoid it. It's back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: However, towards the end, it says that this person is in Glogova 2, and it says "ICMP protocol, 1935/03." Can you see that in the one-but -last column?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just note that General Tolimir has predicated his question on the statement that the DOD, corresponding to the military records, represents the date of death. I can see that the caption of the table itself reads: "Cases of inconsistent date of death/disappearance." I'm not sure what General Tolimir is predicating his statement on, the fact that DOD in the military records means "date of death" rather than "date of disappearance," but I think that's material particularly in presenting the question to the witness in terms of an inconsistency with the, as you can see in the following column, corrected date, or the date -- or any other date relating to the person's disappearance in the record. So if he can at least provide some basis for his assertion that the DOD in the military records means date of death, I think that will be helpful. And it will also provide a clearer basis from which the witness can respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. The headline clearly indicates that DOD seems to be inconsistent date of death/disappearance, and we have heard the witness about that. With that addition, are you able to answer the last question? If you recall it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I don't recall what I was -- what I'm being asked to respond to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a long time ago. It has already disappeared from the screen. Could you please repeat your last question, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I just had some questions. I didn't make any assertions. Look at everything that I've said and it will be clear. I only ask questions. So I will repeat my question now. I will repeat my question. Were indications given to the ICMP regarding discrepancy between the information that comes from the ICMP records and other records, for example, that of the BH army? And I mentioned an example here; namely, the BH army has a person as disappeared or died on the 10th of January, 1994, that is, a year before the events in Srebrenica, and in your protocol this person is registered as having been found in Glogova 2. So now I am waiting for your answer, whether that was reported or indicated to you or not.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in any systematic manner. As I said before, our information comes from reports of the family. With regard to the discrepancy, was this individual -- we don't -- we're not responsible for or know about the Bosnian army records. For example, looking at this, it's not clear to me whether that is the -- 1994 is the date at which they last saw that individual. That to say, their date of disappearance. So whether there's an actual discrepancy, to me, is not clear at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Parsons. This list has a database based on which it was made, and it was made by the expert of the Prosecution. And there appears to be a discrepancy between the information that the OTP has and what the army has and, again, with what you put in that last column. Now did anyone from the International Tribunal direct your attention to these discrepancies, that is, by the OTP, since this was made by their expert for the Prosecution? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge that this list, per se, has been brought to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons, for your answer. Could you answer this question: If the ICMP were to receive documents or statements that indicate that there is information about the date of death and that the date of death was wrongly recorded in the BH army or in the Missing Persons Institute that you mentioned or the ICMP, and if that were the case, which of all this information would finally be relevant?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our database reflects the information that we have collected from families. We have not undertaken to do a comprehensive investigation of the status of missing persons in Bosnia. And so our data that we obtained from families would -- would remain as such. And, in fact, that information is -- is not critical with regard to our primary effort to identify these individuals. The issue of reported date of disappearance is one that is basically impossible to resolve. We see, even, an example of it here, where I made reference to it being very unclear what it means to call the date of disappearance of someone in 1994. And we faced this problem as well. We'll obtain samples from multiple family members and each of them will provide information on what they know of the date and place of disappearance. And different of those family members may, in fact, have -- provide somewhat different information. One of them may have last seen the family member two days before the fall of Srebrenica when he was left at the DutchBat compound or something like that, and another family member may have seen him a couple of days after. So these are records that are extremely difficult to resolve, and we don't undertake a systematic effort to try to resolve all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If the family has a document issued by a court that says a certain person was killed on such and such a date, for example, in 1994, as it says here, and then based on that they obtain certain privileges such as retirement or social welfare and you made an entry in the final column that this particular person had been found in Glogova, how is that problem going to be resolved? Can you answer that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't see that this document indicates a report that this individual was killed on -- in 1994. But, in any case, if a family came to us to update the information that they had provided, we would enter it. None of that would likely affect our conclusion, based on scientific identification processes, that that individual was in fact recovered from Glogova 2. I think the fact that we were able to provide a definitive scientific identification of the individual from Glogova 2 would in fact be the appropriate resolution to any discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons. When we get to the scientific analysis and molecules, I will ask you questions that are relevant to what you just said. But please tell us how to resolve this problem, namely, that in one entry the person is listed as being in a mass grave and in 1994 he is in the military records or municipal records as having died and then the family gets certain welfare. Is the family going to have to return all the welfare because that person was recorded as having been killed, and is that your responsibility? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of the basis of this list; and I don't know anything about family reparations and welfare; and, no, it is not our responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just for the record, I don't see any indication or recording ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see in this list any entry, any recording, of killing of the people. We have only the column "date of death" or "date of disappearance." Nothing about killing. I just wanted to put that on the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, if someone was to provide you with this list, or a list like this, where there are discrepancies, where the army refused to change its attitude based on the documents that it has, and here the entries of the ICMP remain the same, then does the ICMP claim that that particular person was found in Glogova, and is that information then valid?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would remain the ICMP's conclusion that the individual was obtained from Glogova. We're always happy to look -- to review our cases should credible information come to our attention that would suggest some real discrepancy. I don't view these sort of mishmash of lists as something that would flag major scientific review of our cases. But, in general, the ICMP considers that these global issues relating to lists of missing persons is the domain of the Missing Persons Institute which is, in fact, in the process of establishing a central list of missing persons to resolve exactly these sorts of issues. And we've provided our information to the Missing Persons Institute to assist them in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't ask any more questions about this. This is the last one: If there are witnesses to the death that the army has -- and Mr. Brunborg said that the BH army refused to change its attitude, then would you still -- would you still claim that this -- that particular person was found in Glogova? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes. Seeing someone being killed and knowing where his remains are -- are different things from -- to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If, in this Court, we as the Defence say that there are several such case - Mr. Brunborg mentioned 220 such cases - are you in any way whatsoever obliged to check and correct the entries that you've made in relation to a particular person? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think that the question comports with the evidence or the statements of Dr. Brunborg. I think the suggestion that General Tolimir is making here is that there are 220 cases where somebody has witnessed the death or has concrete information of a death that is inconsistent with the date of disappearance as is indicated in this record. I don't believe that that is correct, and I don't believe that reflects Dr. Brunborg's testimony, or the report for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Parsons, the question was, in fact: Are you in any way obliged to check and correct the entries that you've made in relation to a particular person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not feel obliged to do that necessarily in this case. It depends upon the -- the basis of the evidence that underlies this that would trigger, for us, enough concern to go and investigate our previous work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons. I won't ask any more questions about this. The Trial Chamber will make its decision based on what we heard. My next question is: Who submits to the ICMP samples from exhumed bodies for purposes of DNA analysis? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would remind the Court of my extensive address of this issue yesterday. But samples are submitted to the ICMP under the auspices of court-appointed pathologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, is that this Tribunal or the national Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The national authorities in Bosnia or state authorities; whoever has appropriate jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic case, P1936 - P1935 is the version under seal - at page number 20875, lines 16 through 18, you said the following, and I'm quoting your words: "In the Srebrenica case, a decision was made to take two nominal denominations" [as interpreted] "in that area because the confusing nature of the events makes it difficult to arrive at a consistent date of disappearance or place of disappearance ..." I was reading what you said word for word, and I'll put my question to you based on how I understand your -- what you said. Who was it within the ICMP who decided that nominal and not actual dates of a person's disappearance be given? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been the staff involved from the ICMP's identification coordination division whose staff was involved in taking statements and reference blood samples from the families. And, indeed, when you interview multiple family members associated with the same missing person to obtain information concerning the date and place of disappearance, we will, here, consider the events of the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995, virtually every family member may or, very commonly, will provide slightly divergent information regarding the last date that they saw the individual or where they -- where they think he went missing. And it wound up being a body of information that we had not the investigative capacity or, in fact, mission to try to sort out. We were obtaining information that would allow us to assist in the identification of these individuals. So faced with this massive process of registry and blood sample collection, the -- the staff members there adopted basically a shorthand for -- for indicating that the families are basically reporting the individual missing from the fall of Srebrenica and classified it more generally into one of -- of two primary components of the event, either the missing person -- the information with regard to this categorisation was much more consistent and less difficult to resolve, either that person wound up going to the DutchBat centre near Potocari or that individual was one of the very large column of men who fled from Srebrenica in the days preceding July 11th and 12th. So we don't have recorded extremely precise information in that -- with regard to those categories because there's so much minor divergence, and it would be a matter of adding all kinds of different columns to the table that simply wouldn't be informative, given the level of investigation that actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Let's be precise. It was, therefore, for the sake of your own purposes within the ICMP that nominal and not actual dates be listed, in order for you to more easily apply your method. Your data, which, in this case is nominal, is it then relevant and used for court purposes for the sake of establishing facts? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I basically agree with the first part of your statement with regard to these are practical measures that we have undertaken so that we can most efficiently proceed with our effort to identify these people. And I simply leave it to the Court to determine what it wants to conclude with regard to the nature of our information as we have, in our best faith, provided it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons. Was the same rule regarding nominal dates and places of disappearance used more generally in your work or was it only the case with the Srebrenica missing? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is generally the case that the ICMP doesn't consider -- does not conduct what it considers to be full-fledged investigations regarding the date and place of disappearance, but it is the case that the Srebrenica event is unique in terms of its magnitude and the number of families affected. So I'm unaware of any other systematic use of nominal data in the manner that -- that we're discussing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for saying that it is not up to your commission to establish the date and place of disappearance. Rather, you only set them out in nominal terms. Now, the information that the ICMP receives, is it neutral in terms of the manner of death? For instance, whether an individual met his death in combat or otherwise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's quite a bit -- I'm sorry for my delay in responding. There's quite a few components that might be addressed in response to this -- to this question. As you know, the ICMP is involved in scientific evacuations of many graves related to Srebrenica and the anthropological examination of remains that come from those graves and through our formal association with the court-appointed pathologist at Podrinje Identification Project, who for many years were -- played a dual role as an ICMP employee and as a state-appointed pathologist. We have a lot of information regarding the cause of death of individuals from Srebrenica. The DNA data that we have been discussing and the information from the families, of course, doesn't provide any information regarding manner -- cause or manner of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, on direct examination, you said that you used family blood samples of the person that went missing in order to identify that person through DNA analysis. My question is this: Which of the family members are taken into consideration for sampling for these blood samples? I understood you to say that the mother was the most desirable blood donor. But I'd like to know what is the circle of family members that is acceptable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the general rule is first-order relatives or siblings. So parents or offspring are the best. Siblings are the next best. And then more distant relatives are useful depending upon the combination with regard to other references that are available. So, in fact, all four grandparents are quite useful; two grandparents not nearly as much so. And so we will collect samples from a wide range of -- of relatives. They may not be sufficient or -- or, on the other hand, they may not be necessary, but we prefer to collect widely in case those samples may help. So, you know, things like uncles and aunts generally provide only minor assistance and would be useful only in combination with other family members. But in many cases they are useful, so we're careful to collect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the event that there are no parents, grandparents, or siblings available, how would you go about identifying an individual, and on the basis of which donor sample?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can give you a specific and more general answer to that question. I understand the nature of the question. If you had no parents or grandparents but you had the wife of the missing person and one or more offspring, those would be very useful. But that was just a specific response to the -- to your question as posed. The answer, more generally, is, we'll use whatever relatives we have. And if we don't have enough relatives, it is in fact the case that we won't be able to make an identification at a sufficient level of certainty. And in fact that's one of the primary reasons why we would fail to identify a DNA profile that we've obtained from a victim sample. Either there are no references for that individual or there are insufficient references for that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain how a wife can be a donor? How can it be related to the missing person at all?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very good question that people often ask. An individual -- the DNA loci, the places within the DNA, that we test are located on chromosomes. And everybody has two pairs of each chromosome, one that they inherited from the mother and one that they inherited from the father. So -- and in each of these loci that we look at - they're independent from each other; there's 15 of them - an individual chromosome may have any number of variations. So this is the source of variation that distinguishes one person from the next. So if we have an individual who is missing and we have his offspring, that offspring got half of his DNA from his father and half of his DNA from his mother. So if this individual's missing, if we have both the offspring and the mother, that allow us to deduce the genetics types of the father. So it's -- these people are -- all have DNA in combination with one another that can be interpreted very, very usefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can I take it that this is only possible if there are children.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct. If there are no children, the spouse is an unrelated individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons. Can you tell us if in that case any other evidence is necessary in terms of whether the wife had a child by that missing person within wedlock? Does there have to be some sort of proof to that effect? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We -- we make the identifications based on the information provided to us by families. It would certainly be abhorrently intrusive to try to delve into issues such as you refer to. We are trying to provide the families with their missing loved ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand what you're saying. But what if such a sample takes you in the wrong direction, where you are unable to find the wife's or husband's chromosome in children? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general that would give rise to our inability to identify that individual. It's sadly the case that we're not able to identify everybody killed in these conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, how many cases have you had so far where you were unable to identify an individual because you didn't have a sufficient number of chromosomes or the certainty wasn't at 99 per cent, as you said yesterday? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just checking if I have listed here the information that would allow me to give you a specific answer to that question. It doesn't appear that I do. In general, with regard -- the way I would address your question is to say: How many DNA profiles of unique individuals have we obtained from victim samples that we have not been able to match to family reference samples. And that is a number that's available. It actually takes some time for us to generate it. And I'm sorry, I don't have that information here. There are quite a few. With regard to samples considered to be related to Srebrenica, however, we have more specific information. And we have about a 96 per cent match rate on victim profiles from -- from graves considered associated with Srebrenica. So that's really quite a remarkable statistic and indicates that we in fact have very good representation of the population missing from Srebrenica by the family members. Let me say again what I meant by that. If a sample comes to us from a grave associated with Srebrenica and it produced a DNA profile we have not seen before, there's a 96 per cent chance that we will find a match for it amongst individuals who have reported a missing loved one from the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the ICMP identify the Srebrenica missing from samples taken from distant relatives? And, if so, can you tell us what is the lineage of the most distant relatives that would still allow for identification? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think we don't know what is meant by distant relatives without me getting more specific. But I don't want to quibble. In -- generally, distant relatives aren't useful, unless you have them in constellation with at least a small number of closer relatives. And by distant, I'll say cousins, without people that are -- without additional relatives that are closer, generally aren't very useful. Aunts and uncles aren't very useful. We would never be able to identify someone simply by a reference as a cousin, using the technology that we use. One thing that I think I'll add to that, that's worth having in mind, is that identifications can occur in a processive manner. So if we have references for a particular missing individual and that individual is identified, we now then know the genetic profile of that missing person. If that missing person also has additional relatives that are missing, his profile can now be used as a reference sample to identify other related missing persons. So we know the profile of this person that was previously missing and we can use it now as a reference sample. And that's quite useful in the case of Srebrenica because we have so many relatives that are missing together. In many instances, all the male relatives in a family will have been exterminated in this event, and we're able to -- to perform serial identifications in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain for us, please, what the electropherograms are and what is their significance in the DNA analysis? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it won't be helpful for me to try to go into much detail with regard to how electropherograms are generated and what the molecular biology and the chemistry is behind the instrumentation. So I will start simply and then we can build from there if there requires additional clarification. But the electropherograms are a visual representation of the chromosomal loci that I referred to previously. And so each of these loci is associated with character states of varying size. So the electropherogram separates the different loci by virtue of the fact that they happen to be different sizes. And then indicates, by a visual depiction, a peak, and that peak represents when a molecule goes by. And it's labelled in a way that can you see it. So what an electropherogram then is, is from -- for our purposes, would be a visual representation of the genetic type of these individuals, showing the different alleles, those are the different variants, that occur within a particular locus, which is a different position on the chromosome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you receive a bone sample of an individual killed, or dead, what is it that you look for in that sample in order to make a match with a donor sample?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, general DNA is extracted from the remains. So all the DNA that the individual has is taken out. And then procedures are -- molecular biological procedures are performed in small test tubes that cause just the loci we're interested in to be amplified in a way that we can determine the type. Once that happens, it's run on an instrument and we receive the electropherogram. And electropherogram, basically, is a depiction of the raw data upon which we will base our genetic typing of the individual to arrive at, in the case of the electropherograms, a series of coloured peaks that depict the genetic type and those are translated into an allelic numerical designation such as we saw listed on the DNA match reports yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said yesterday that a living molecule needed to be found in the dead sample that you receive. And is it then that the living molecule is compared to the family samples, the donor samples?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We may have some translation issues here. I -- let me clarify what I said. The -- the word that's been translated to me is living, and that's not the proper term. It's not a matter of being alive or not. It is whether or not -- so DNA is a chemical molecule of some complexity. And it's actually quite robust, so it can exist outside of life within a bone sample, for example, without being degraded down to its elemental components. On the other hand, certain environmental conditions cause the DNA to be degraded and it basically disappears as a functional DNA molecule. So I think I used the word "surviving DNA." That just simply means the DNA molecules that have not been degraded environmentally. And so to follow to the second part, yes. But, I mean, what we're able to do is obtain DNA profiles from the deceased individual and compare those to the family members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it is, for everybody, a convenient time for our first break. One last question before --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question. Thank you, Mr. President. It is important because of the follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You just spoke now of a molecule with surviving structures, as it were. Can you tell us if the molecular structure of the bones you use as a sample, the primal aspect of a molecule which can be resurrected, as it were or, rather, which can be used to resurrect a deceased person? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That didn't come through the translation as a clear question, but maybe if I answer it this way, I'll answer what I think you're asking, and that is: If we obtain a DNA profile from a deceased individual, then that represents the DNA that has survived. So, in that case, the fact that we have obtained a profile from it means that the DNA molecular structure has survived, which is well-documented as to being entirely feasible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you to the witness for explaining to us that molecules can survive, which means a great deal to us and our future.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that we should take our break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have our first break now for technical reasons, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, based on what we just said about the molecular structure, my next question would be: Does this mean that in order to verify the accuracy of a DNA report, it is necessary to have an electropherogram based on which the DNA analysis results were obtained?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to do a full scientific technical analysis of the data, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear the interpretation but my assistant told me that the witness gave an affirmative reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the Popovic et al. case, and that's Exhibit 1935, on page 20911, lines 19 to 21, you confirmed that you did not provide any electropherograms. So am I correct in saying that without an electropherogram it is not possible to examine whether the DNA results for missing persons are accurate or whether there is anything missing from them?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Popovic trial, we provided quite a number of electropherograms related to the DNA case files from Bisina, as was requested from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you've answered my next question. So how many electropherograms did you provide in the Popovic case? Did you select them, or was the selection made by one of the sides in the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall how many electropherograms were in there. That would have been dozens. And the request was made for -- to supply the DNA case files related to us through the Office of the Prosecutor for those specific files.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be the same procedure if this Defence sought that certain electropherograms be provided? Would the Defence have to ask for this to be done through the Prosecution and the Court?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem to me that channelling such a request through the Court would be the most appropriate way to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons. In that case, could the Defence make the selection in that case? Or would you make the selection? In case the Defence wanted to challenge some things or prove certain things, could it make the selection?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point of the conversation, I think it's important to establish some of the considerations that go into provision of what the ICMP considers to be protected genetic data. When we obtain concept from families to process their samples and obtain DNA profiles, we make a solemn assurance to them that their sample won't be used for any other purpose than the identification of their loved one. And any other provision of that data would require express consent on the part of the families. Currently, since, I believe, 2007, the consent forms we use allow the family to indicate whether they would permit their genetic profiles to be released with -- in -- in court proceedings such as this one. Prior to 2007, we did not have that blanket provision on the consent form. So a vast majority of our samples are not covered by such a consent. And we know for a fact that the families have great concern in turning over genetic profiles, their personal genetic information, to individuals who they consider complicit in the death of their family members. So in order to provide the samples, the ICMP would have to go to great effort and involving additional trauma to families to specifically seek consent from them to provide the information. With that in mind, and the fact that this is highly technical information that can take years to review, given the vast amount of genetic data that we have, the ICMP would -- would seek to determine that a reasonable course of provision of data was followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons, for mentioning this. My question is this: Could the Court be entrusted with this information with the obligation that they consider this confidential, just as the -- the documents we looked at a moment ago that were also -- that was -- that were also confidential? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of specific consent from the family members, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that the will of the families is limited even in the case of information that was provided to the Prosecution for the purposes of analysis and which was present -- and information which was presented in court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The translation I'm reading of that question has the phrase "the will of the families is limited ..." I don't know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll repeat my question. Can the families limit this Court from getting information that they already have from the Prosecution through some lists that were used for Court purposes and which the Defence wishes to check? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The previous conversation related to electropherograms which contains the actual genetic data of the families, and the Court has not received any such data without the express consent of family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that your commission for which you're working is untouchable by the courts because it is protecting information? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm not quite sure what know what the word "untouchable" means. Certainly we're willing and able to provide information within the bounds of the personal data protection assurances that we have already given to the families to assist the Court and to assist the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, then, can the Court or the Defence or the Prosecution have the obligation to protect this data that you provide, the same way as you are obliged? Or are there no guarantees to that effect? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would class those as legal questions to which I have no expertise or insight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons. Then I'll ask you something else. Since you're testifying here as an expert and not as a regular witness, was -- did the Prosecution direct your attention to the fact that in order to ensure the confidentiality of the reports that you present to the Court as an expert, you must base the evidence that you give on clear indicators?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "Reliability" and not "confidentiality" of the reports.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, my assistant said that I was not interpreted correctly. I would like to repeat because I might have spoken too fast. May I repeat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters already corrected themselves. And they replaced the word "confidentiality" by "reliability." And I think in that context the question is quite clear. I don't see a need for repetition. Sir, are you able to provide Mr. Tolimir with your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One moment. I find elements of the question, notwithstanding the clarification of the interpreter, to be vague. Reports -- "in order to ensure the reliability of the reports that you present to the Court"; I'm not sure what he's meant by "reports." And: "Base ... evidence ... on clear indicators"; I'm not quite sure what that means either. With regard to those -- that specific language, I don't recall that the Prosecution has given me any advice regarding that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, perhaps you rephrase your question and help the witness to understand you in a better way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you to the witness. Were you advised that the sources of the data that you use in court must be clearly indicated and available? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall specifically being advised to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you were not advised, is it your obligation as an expert to make sure that your sources are clearly indicated and available for the analyses that you perform here in court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that contradict the fact that you did not provide us with all the electropherograms for the analyses that you did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm afraid I do object to that question. There has been no request by the Defence heretofore, if I'm using the term correctly, for the provision of any such material. In fact, the electropherograms that Dr. Parsons referred to relating to the Bisina executions were provided to the Defence. They've had that since ... for a long time. Probably better than a year. And there's been no request, even having that information, for any further information for the purpose of analysis, for the purposes of comparisons, for the purposes of extrapolations that they might otherwise make, or for the purposes of any expert they might intend to call. So I think that the question is unfair as put to the witness, particularly since it's clearly predicated on the fact that there was no such request made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you get the floor, Mr. Gajic, I would like to have an explanation for the statement in the last question: "... the fact that you did not provide us with all the electropherograms for the analyses that you did?" I would like to know what that means. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that Mr. Tolimir's question is very clear. It was put in the context of general practice, that the sources a particular expert uses for the compilation of a list or an analysis should be indicated and available. And this question was formulated in relation to that rule. Mr. Vanderpuye said that there was no specific request for the electropherograms, that the Defence didn't make such a request; that is correct. Such a request has not been filed yet. However, we consider it the obligation of the expert to indicate the sources that he used during the compilation of his report and to submit them together with that report, to submit them to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would submit as follows, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please. I would like to draw your attention again on the wording of this question: "Does that contradict the fact that you" -- excuse me, please listen. "... the fact that you did not provide us with all the electropherograms ..." I would like to know what do you mean by "you" and what do you mean by "us" to make it clear for all parties. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tolimir used the phrase "us," whether it be the Defence, the Prosecution, or the Court. Either of the parties. Either of the parties to the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In your understanding, was that - I just wanted to know that - an obligation by this expert witness to provide the Defence directly with information and data?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To all the parties, not only the Defence. Our understanding is that when an expert submits a report, he must clearly indicate the documentation and the sources that they used in order to write the report. And in this case, what we would be dealing with are very large lists. And then it would be clear what the source is, and this source should be clearly indicated and readily available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is now much more clear. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There are two issues that arise from this, Mr. President. The first thing is the so-called rule that Mr. Gajic is referring to. I'm unaware of any such rule in our jurisprudence or in any other jurisprudence concerning the availability in the form of the production of the records for the purposes of the Defence regarding for analytical purposes or for any other purpose. That's number one. There is no such rule. The second thing is, there's a difference between the availability of the material and the production of the material. There's nothing in this record that suggests that this material is unavailable or has been unavailable to the Defence to inspect. The reason why they don't have it, first and foremost, is because they never asked for it. The second thing is that they do have in their possession several electropherograms which they can examine, they can test, and they can determine the reliability in general from which to extrapolate the reliability of the match list that's been provided by ICMP concerning the Srebrenica-related graves, and those are the Bisina-related case files. I think there are 39 or 38 of them that they have. All of these files contain the electropherograms upon which the identifications and the matches were made. I can address those in redirect examination since we have one such file already in evidence. The other issue relates to the fact that Dr. Parsons did produce a report which is also in evidence - I don't have the number in front of me - but it is an ICMP methodology report that goes from 2001 to 2008. In that report it specifically refers to the standard operating procedures that were employed by the ICMP in the DNA identification process during that period of time. All of those standard operating procedures are specifically referenced in the document as I -- as I mentioned in my summary at the beginning of his testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please, listen to Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- as I mentioned in the summary in the beginning of my [sic] testimony. Okay. The methodology report, I understand, is 65 ter 2361. I don't recall what the P number is. But it references the standard operating procedures that were followed in -- in processing the -- the DNA profiles for the purposes of matching. All of them are referred to in that report. The Defence has had access to that report for a long time. They've had access to the standard operating procedures for a long time. Those you can see, even in the exhibit list, are numerous documents that show the kinds of instrumentation that's used, the manner in which the DNA is processed, the process of intaking it, matching it, declaring matches. All of this is in Dr. Parsons's report. So to say that that material which is relied upon is not identified or available is, frankly, not accurate, to say the least. And I think that Mr. Gajic knows that. And if we're talking specifically about the availability of electropherograms, this is an issue which arose also in the Popovic case. It's also arisen in the Karadzic case. Where, in the Karadzic case, a specific request was made to have that material available, which ultimately was never communicated to the ICMP by the Karadzic Defence. And the same is true in this case. Worse in this case is that no communication has been made by the Defence even to the Office of the Prosecutor to attempt to have the ICMP produce that material or a request made to the ICMP directly to -- to have access to that material, to have it available. The Defence is aware that there is certain confidential information contained in those case files and that an extraordinary amount of work has to go in to try and secure the necessary consents in order to get family members who have depended upon the confidentiality of that material to help them identify their loved ones; they know this. And to bring it up at this stage of the proceedings and suggest that it hasn't been made available to them I think is unfair and it's predicated on an inaccurate record, one that I think the evidence clearly refutes. And I just want to that be clear. If they have such a request, it would be helpful if they had raised it well in advance of this. Because this takes months and months and months of work on the part of the ICMP to try to accommodate. Even the 39 files that we managed to get in the Popovic case took months and months and months because it's a lot of leg work that has to be done to contain this consent. And I think -- I think Mr. Gajic is aware of that. Certainly, if he'd read the record of the Popovic case he would be. So I think it's an unfair position to put the witness in. I think it's a misstatement of Law of the Tribunal. And it's also a misrepresentation of the facts concerning the provision of those records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Gajic, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the first point regarding the rules whereby the sources on which an expert report is based should be clearly referenced and made readily available is well-established before -- this is the rule which is well-established before this Tribunal, and I don't think I'll need much time to obtain it. As for the availability of the ICMP data, well, it's clear from the Popovic transcript and from my conversations with the individuals involved in the Defence teams in the Popovic case that the material is very difficult to obtain. We've also been able to hear from the expert here that some of the electropherograms are not available at all. And it was within that context that the question was formulated. The witness gave a clear answer that there were such concern difficulties, and I'll paraphrase. My understanding of what he said was that it was almost impossible to provide the parties to a proceeding with all the electropherograms. So why should be seeking them if it's impossible? We are merely exploring the possibility of access to the material. What we are raising here is a methodological question of how the findings in the report can be verified. We haven't named any names. We haven't accused the ICMP of failing to accommodate any of our requests. We are quite clear on what the position of the ICMP is and we were able to learn that from the previous cases. The material we received from the Popovic case is something that we looked at while preparing for this case. We received them roughly at the same time when the Defence teams of the Popovic case received them. But that's not enough. That's a couple of dozen electropherograms chosen by the ICMP, according to the information I have, or that, at least, is my understanding. That is absolutely insufficient to check a list containing thousands upon thousands of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I see you are still on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am on my feet, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would suggest that if the Defence seeks access to this information that we meet with them, or they can meet with us. I think we can sort this issue out without using up valuable Court time. The question, as I objected to it, was -- the basis of my objection was because it was suggestive of the fact that the Defence was deprived of information that they should otherwise have received. I understand Mr. Gajic's clarification. And I think with that understanding we can go forward. We'll talk with the Defence and work out the disposition of their -- maybe they have a request, maybe they don't, for this material, but I think we can proceed so that we don't use up any more time on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In my understanding, this is a very reasonable proposal. Mr. Gajic, you want to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll respond very briefly. The Defence will file appropriate requests, of course. This is an ongoing trial. We will be hearing this witness, but the trial isn't over yet. And we will be approaching you on this issue once this witness has testified. I do believe that Mr. Tolimir is entitled to put the sort of question he formulated. He wants to see what the practice of writing the reports was and what the possibilities for checking the data contained in the reports are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to suggest that the parties liaise and meet and try to come to a common understanding. And it's, of course, open for the Defence to file any motion in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may do what is your interest of your client. We should continue the cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is what I'd like to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does the OTP have a monopoly over the data that he, as an expert, used for the purposes of the analysis presented before the Trial Chamber? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
