utterances.text: Thank you. Were the lists - and I emphasise the lists - of the ICMP of confidential nature; and, if so, why? And I'm referring to the lists, not the electropherograms.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis for requesting that the lists be kept confidential, as they reflect a list of names of individuals on DNA match reports, relates to, again, the privacy of the traumatised families involved, particularly with regard to the issue of their notification of their loved one's death and information relating to its case. We would not want a family to first become aware that their family member has been DNA matched through watching these court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons. I asked you clearly to tell -- to tell me about the lists and not about the matches or the electropherograms. My question was why the lists of those missing from Srebrenica themselves are of confidential nature. And I mean the lists that do not include any family names or the data contained in electropherograms.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lists that we provide do contain the family names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The ICRC also provides names of those missing. So why are their lists in the public domain and yours are not? Can you explain this for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list that we provided that, has been discussed greatly, is not a list of the missing; it's the list of the identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the list of the identified. I was asking you about the list of the missing persons that you keep as confidential. Why is that so?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what -- you'll have to specify. What list of missing persons? I am unaware of any that has been presented or discussed here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm referring to the same list that is kept by the ICRC, the list of missing persons that is then used for the purposes of this Tribunal. Does your institution, the ICMP, does it not keep a list of missing persons? After all, that is your name.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. It's more clear now. Yes, as I have indicated earlier, we have a list of persons reported to the ICMP missing as a result of the conflict and -- and for which we have received genetic reference samples. I -- I beg the pardon of the Court that I'm not positive what the ICMP's position is regarding the confidentiality of that list itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand your position, so I will not belabour the point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D597 shown in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for it to appear, let me tell you that that's a document, according to the information that we have, that you provided to the OTP. It's titled: "A comprehensive overview or list of technical procedures related to DNA processes at the International Commission for Missing Persons." The report was created on the 14th of April, 2010. This is my question: Can you tell us, why was it asked of you to draw up a report of this sort? And when I say "you," I mean the commission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not asked of us to draw up this report. This report was drawn up upon our own request. And it was intended to provide an independent analysis an information by leading experts in the world of forensic science, relating to the identification or the DNA match by the ICMP of Colonel Avdo Palic, of the remains of Colonel Avdo Palic, and the match of a DNA profile from him to his family members. With regard to this case, it is unfortunate that the ICMP had obtained a bone sample from Colonel -- what proved to be Colonel Palic in 2001 and generated a DNA profile from that bone sample in 2002 that should have been able to affect a DNA match at that time. Due to an extremely unusual combination of human clerical error in sample name entry into an instrument and a completely unanticipated software glitch, as we've come to call it, with regard to how data was subsequently output from the instrument, the result of that unusual combination was that the DNA profile was entered into the ICMP comparison database in an incorrect form, one that prevented it from being matched. And this occasioned a very unfortunate delay in the discovery of this match, which was not identified until 2009. The reason it was discovered in 2009 is because, under my direction, the ICMP, with a constant emphasis on doing the best work that we can, instituted a full technical review of all previously unmatched DNA profiles from the early periods of the ICMP operation. So all DNA profiles from victim samples that had not matched any family references underwent a full de novo technical review with the aim of seeing if there was any improvements we could make in those genetic profiles as a result of improved technical capabilities or additional runs of the data, in order to find matches. We found very, very few cases where additional identifications could be made out of these 1.582 unmatched profiles that we examined. One of them was -- allowed us -- one of them was the case of Colonel Palic. We found the cause of the -- of the lack of previous identification, and we were very concerned about that delay. And moreover, we were concerned about the perceptions that such a delay would -- might be occasioned amongst stakeholders and families regarding the ICMP's work. Many, many people continue to wait anxiously for the identification of their loved ones and -- and a delay of such a magnitude in an identification would occasion concern. So with regard to that, and with an emphasis on full transparency within the bounds of personal data protection that has already been discussed, we invited a team of highly regarded international experts to perform a full independent review of the cause of the delay of the identification of Colonel Palic, as well as an open-ended and wide-ranging investigation as to the extent to which the problems involved in the Palic case could be seen to be systematic, the extent to which similar problems might have occurred, and the extent to which, in general, the ICMP's system is effective, reliable, responsible, ethical, and conducted with high integrity. And that is the nature of the report that is -- that's placed in front of the Court today, right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, what is the customary period that lapses from the moment a sample is taken for the DNA analysis to the moment the DNA results are obtained? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll talk about some of the factors that influence the amount of time it takes to make a DNA match. First of all, it depends upon the back-log of DNA samples that we have. Particularly in the early days of ICMP's operation, we had vast numbers of bone samples available for DNA typing. These would be -- these would come from operations at the ICTY and other mass graves that had been exhumed to the point where our high throughput DNA laboratory process took some months in order to -- to process the back-log. Today, there's a much less delay between obtaining a sample and producing a DNA profile from that sample. Minimally, it might be several weeks. It's not unusual for it to take longer, given that any given sample is in process with a large number of other samples. So in general, weeks to months, a small number of months, delay between obtaining a sample and obtaining a DNA profile from it should it be possible to obtain such a profile. Some cases are difficult and require multiple attempts to extract the DNA. Sometimes we'll even request that an additional sample be sent from the same case because -- to further augment the quality and quantity of DNA that we receive from the case. So there are many variables that go into it. So far I have spoken only about obtaining a DNA profile from a bone sample. With regard to making a match, there are additional steps involved. And one absolutely critical component is that there has to be family reference samples that the DNA profile from the victim can match. So if we already have family reference samples in the database and we obtain a DNA profile and upload it to the database, generally that match will be found very, very quickly, because the computerised processes are largely automatic. And then it would take on the order of maybe a couple of additional weeks for all the appropriate review processes to occur. Now, it wouldn't take that long if we had only one case to worry about, but we operate in a very large batch mode, and so that's why -- that's what accounts for the time-periods that I'm representing as typical. In the case of Colonel Palic, in fact we did not obtain family reference samples that would permit his identification until 2005. So, actually, when we first obtained a DNA profile from that bone sample in 2002, we would not have been able to match it until 2005. And that is exemplary of a reason why in many instances there is a many-year delay between obtaining a bone profile from the victim and obtaining a match because we don't yet have the requisite family reference samples. They continue to come in. When they get them, they go into the database and then a match will be very quickly made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, I tried to pick out the actual conclusion and what it was out of the answer you gave me. So can you answer me next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that, can we have page 7 of this report shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On that page there is question number one. And I'm quoting: "Why has it been seven years between the time the 9100507 bone DNA profile was entered into the database and the 2009 match to Colonel Palic's relatives?" You've just told us that you received the donor samples only in 2005. So can you please describe for us the nature of the error which occurred in the procedure related to this particular sample, with the bar code 9100507? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I'll be able to give you some indication of that. I would also like to note, as this report is in evidence in the court, that an extremely detailed and comprehensive description is present in this report. And I would not be capable in any way of expanding or making it more clear than what is written here. And I fear that if I try to go through the explanation in substantial detail that will we'll be bogged down in some technical procedures that will probably not mean very much to the Court and take a great deal of time. With that said, I have no objection to any depth that we would like do go into. But let me take a -- an attempt at an abbreviated and, I hope, clear explanation of basically what happened. In fact, I already made reference to it. When a sample is loaded onto the primary instrument that provides the DNA profile, the software that runs that instrument require -- that was run at that time requires the sample name to be entered into two different places in the -- with regard to a particular sample. This -- this 9100507 sample actually was entered correctly in the two places, where you have to put the same information in two separate spots. However, the sample following that was run on the same instrument had its correct number added. But inadvertently, as a result of human error, in the second place where that person had to indicate the sample, it was erroneously entered as this 9100507. The instrument was then run and an output of the DNA data was generated, and in -- in a phenomenon, if you will, that was completely unknown and completely -- by anyone that I'm aware of, certainly unknown to the ICMP and unanticipated by the ICMP, is that instead of some kind of an error message associated with this incorrect entry, the computer instead exported a hybrid profile for 9100507 that contained part of the information from the authentic sample and part of the information from the following sample, creating a hybrid genetic profile that was not capable of being matched to the Palic reference samples when they came in 2005. That's the -- that's the primary cause of the problem. I will say, also, that there would be -- a secondary cause to the problem is that that was not detected via a review process. It -- it -- it should have been but it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 10, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I'm quoting from it. You can read it for yourself. "Data review is one of many quality control mechanisms that help identify and prevent incorrect DNA profiles from being uploaded to a database. Documentation from 2001 was not available to verify either the existence of a review procedure," et cetera. This is my question: What sort of documentation from 2001 is referred to here and why was it not available?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the ICMP standard operating procedures did not unambiguously delineate what the -- what the review process should have been. That was prior to ICMP's accreditation and also prior to continuing development of highly specific standard operating procedures that would have been able to indicate precisely what was done at that time. The paragraph continues, immediately following the section that was just read, that was: "Anecdotally, the panel" - that's the expert panel in conducting this elevations - "was informed that in order for a DNA profile from the unidentified human remains to be submitted by the Sarajevo laboratory," et cetera, "a review process would have been conducted." So we were able to interview people present in the laboratory at that time. And even though the procedures were not documented, it was the general practice that the type of error that occurred here should have been caught. So it was a deficiency in what was the standard practice at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And my question is this: This checking of the DNA sample that was taken from mass graves, as we can see, based on this text, it was done by Esma Palic. It says on this page: "In 2007, Ms. Esma Palic submitted in writing a request to the ICMP to reinvestigate specific bones from the Vragolovi grave-site." My question is: Are such requests frequent in the practice of the ICMP? And why did Mrs. Palic call these specific bones from the Vragolovi grave-site?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relating to the first part of your question, I'll say that the ICMP gets very large numbers of inquiries from family members checking on the status of their cases, and these can be along the lines of, I gave my blood sample years ago; I still haven't heard anything; what's going on? And we would normally then check the databases to make sure that the family's blood samples are properly in the database, that they reside there, and report back to them that, you know, We're sorry there hasn't been a match. Apparently no victim sample has come to match your individual. So the -- all kinds of inquiries regarding the status of cases come really on almost a daily basis to the ICMP. And that's our relationship with families, that we try to provide with information. So in some respects the request by Mrs. Palic was not particularly unusual of the standpoint of queries that come in to the identification coordination division. But, in fact, the case of Avdo Palic was rather unique in a number of regards, and there was a great deal of international attention addressed to the attempt to recover the remains of Colonel Palic. There's a great deal of investigative activity outside of the ICMP, and we responded on many occasions to evacuations specifically related to the possibility that Colonel Palic might be in a particular grave. So I do not actually know what information came into the possession of Mrs. Palic or the Office of the High Representative relating to this particular grave, called here Vragolovi. But they did have some other information based on other investigations that caused them to inquire of the ICMP to check and see if that could -- if those could be related to Colonel Palic. What happened in response to this inquiry, as far as we've been able to reconstruct, is that the identification coordination division went to the databases to check to determine if a DNA profile was entered for the victim sample, if there were DNA profiles that had been entered for the family samples, and if those DNA profiles were consistent with each other. And, unfortunately, because a incorrect hybrid profile was in the database associated with the sample that came to be identified as Colonel Palic, they, when compared this information, said, No, it's not a match. So when we followed up on that inquiry, it was at the level of the profiles that exist in the database and the fact that as they existed in the database there was not a match. The ICMP would prefer it, in hindsight, if that inquiry had triggered a full technical review of that particular DNA profile, in which case we would have found the error, most likely, and been able to make the identification at that time. Unfortunately, it was not until we conducted our own retrospective analysis, again with the emphasis on doing all we could to resolve as many cases as we can, that we identified the error and reported it as quickly as we could thereupon, after additional rounds of confirmatory testing to make sure that the -- that the problem had been appropriately resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons. Since the initial DNA results of the profile were negative, was the ICMP presented with specific reasons why Mrs. Palic thought that the remains of her husband were in the Vragolovi grave-site?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since there was a number of problems in this case, did the ICMP determine that -- the time of disappearance of Mr. Palic, and did they use their specific methods for that? Or did they have certain information that wasn't contested by either of the sides; in this case, the family?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ICMP did not perform, as far as I'm aware, any investigation into the time of disappearance of Mr. Palic, other than what would have been recorded in the family information such as I had discussed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will repeat my question. You said when he went missing. Did you have information on when he was killed, when he died? Did you have any information about that in your records? Was that provided by the family and those who provided bone samples? Those who were the donors.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We may have been exposed anecdotally to some information; but, no, there was no formal transfer of what I would called evidentiary information. It was -- it's just not the area that we're concerned with. The ICMP has not been engaged in investigating the disappearance of Colonel Palic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 26 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's by this expert panel. And they made some recommendations. And, as we can see, that: "... the quality check of the bone DNA profiles from 2001 to 2004 should be continued to completion." And on page 27, in e-court --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- you say: "Review and validation of the Forensic Data Management System by an independent third party should be continued." Could you explain what you meant by this and who that independent third party is? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reference was made to two separate of the recommendations. The first one you referred to was completion of this retrospective date review, which required a vast amount of effort in terms of identifying samples where we could re-run the tests on the original DNA extract or go back and re-extract DNA from the samples again. It has been a long-standing process, but it has been completed. And, in fact, from these 1.582 profiles that were previously unmatched, we were able to make 16 additional matches. That's a vast amount of work for that level of matching, but we're very pleased to have been able to resolve those cases. It was the conclusion of the expert panel that that -- the level of -- of additional matches that we were able to make was consistent with a process that was highly effect and efficient throughout, and highly reliable. With regard to external validation of our database system called the Forensic Database Management System, we have been pursuing an arrangement with a German company who has reviewed the database with regard to programming characteristics in line with industry standards for software review. And we are now looking into the second phase of this -- this additional quality control validation step of an external party. So, yes, that is in process. That shouldn't be taken to indicate that there's been no form of validation of the Forensic Data Management System. It has undergone a wide -- a large battery of internal user acceptance tests and performance tests, and it is considered by us to be internally validated. We were just looking to -- to continually increase the level of quality-control parameters that we have at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind what you said, when can the parties in this procedure expect a report on such a review?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what review? Oh, the validation of the -- the external validation of the FDMS; is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear to me at this point when that will be completed. Most likely this year. To be honest with you, it's not one of our absolute highest priorities because we think that there's very little risk that this system is causing any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, please tell us whether I am correct if I say that the identification conducted by DNA is too early until --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the end of his question. The interpreter didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreter didn't catch the end of your question. They interpreted only until the words: "The identification conducted by DNA is too early until ..." The rest is missing. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is the identification carried out by DNA considered preliminary until it is confirmed by the pathologist and the family of the missing person?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official finding of death is -- is determined by a pathologist who takes into account the DNA match report. I don't believe that the family of the missing is -- plays a legal role in the determination of death. However, it's -- it's always the case that the family is presented with the information, and a very important component of the identification is the hand-over of the remains to the families.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you said that it's the pathologist who officially determines and decides on the time of death, is that also the case, or was that also the case, with Mr. Palic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You make specific reference to the time of death, and that's not generally something that even a pathologist is going to be able to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If the Court needed us to establish when exactly Mr. Palic was killed, could you give us some advice on how this Court could obtain that information, perhaps through some other organs and commissions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, no. I don't feel like I myself personally could do that. Such information would be dependant upon an investigation involving such things as witnesses, site analyses, et cetera. But I don't -- I'm not in a position, as I sit here, to recommend particular organs or commissions that would be involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us whether DNA analysis can be used to establish the time of death based on the degree of bone decomposition.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, no, there's really not any useful information to be obtained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So, based on what is it determined that somebody disappeared two billion years ago, which is included in some scientific analyses? And they are referring to the decomposition time of uranium that is located in the bones.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're fundamentally confused. Nobody disappeared two billion years ago because humans had not yet evolved, anywhere close to that time. And I don't think that decomposition of uranium in bones is used for any dating.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I wasn't referring to bone decomposition, but the time needed for the decomposition of -- the time of carbonating [as interpreted]. That's what I was referring to. It might have been misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, carbon dating you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert on -- on molecular methods of dating. I'm only peripherally as a scientist exposed to that. Carbon-14 dating, as I am aware, insofar as I'm aware, is not applicable to the time-frames that we're dealing with, with regard to the current conflict -- or, the conflict in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. Thank you for directing us to examine this through some others, through some eye-witnesses perhaps, and for saying that this could not be done through DNA analysis. Could you tell us, what is the usual time-period from the moment a DNA profile is matched by the commission until the families are informed of a particular person having been identified? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably, it would be possible to give you a databased average value. I apologise that I don't have that information available to me now. I would have to confer with and assemble at some effort that information from Dr. Kesetovic at the Podrinje Identification Project. But let me talk a little bit about the factor that affect the time between submission of a DNA match report and the final closure of the case in coordination with the families. The complex grave assemblages associated with Srebrenica, where very large primary graves were established and then by the perpetrators re-exhumed and then buried in a series of clandestine graves throughout the countryside some months later created a situation that has greatly complicated the family notification and case-closure process. Because it is commonly the case for different parts of the same body to have been disassociated and be in separate parts of the same secondary grave or, in many, many instances, also in different secondary graves. And these can be linked together by DNA in some quite comprehensive ways to establish a pattern of linkages between graves, and we have done that. However, with regard to family notifications, we have a situation where, at the mortuary facility, there may be a large series of partial-remains cases being examined and sampled for DNA. Based on all the results already obtained, we know that there's a linkage between one of these graves and several other of the graves, all of which may be in examination at the same time. So I have a situation where a DNA match report is generated, let's say, on the lower leg of an individual; it's highly traumatic to go to the families and say, We've made an identification on a body part of your loved one but we don't know where the remainder of that individual is; and if it's in a situation where it is reasonably anticipated that additional body parts from the same individual will be discovered, sometimes there a delay in notifying the family until we feel like multiple of these grave have been sufficiently examined and tested. Now, that's evolved a little bit, because in the application of that kind of logic, the -- the counter-argument to that type of an approach is that the families are desperately waiting for word of their loved ones, and we don't want to incur undue delay in -- in notification. So it is presently the policy at PIP that the family would be notified relatively directly after the receipt of the first DNA match report. But in the past there has been some delay. And these considerations have been communicated to the families to try to understand what their desires are; would they prefer to wait until most of the individual has been reassociated. And there's a diversity of opinion, but we try to take into account the generally-expressed feelings of the families. But now notification is quite direct after having received the remains. Another component of the case closure -- so that's notification of the families. That's telling the families, We have a DNA report; here's the status of the case; and would you like us to hand these remains over to you? In instances there, the families, even having been notified, may request that the case be remain -- remain open until additional of the remains had been -- have been found. So that's an additional reason why there's some cases where the families have been notified but the case isn't closed yet. And I don't know the -- I don't know the numbers of those. And then lastly, there can be variable delay between obtaining a DNA match and case closure because it simply takes a lot of time to pull all the different cases out. So -- we've found instance where an individual has been reassociated by eight or ten separate body parts all with a unique DNA test. And then that -- all those cases have to be re-examined, the personal effects that may have been associated need to be examined, and it's -- it's a time-consuming process when you're dealing with so many -- so many samples. So that's another reason why there may be a bit of a back-log with regard to case closure. So if I may follow up with what I think is relevant information, currently DNA match reports have been issued by the ICMP on 6.441 individuals reported missing from Srebrenica. With regard to closure of those cases by the legal authorities at the Podrinje Identification Project, the number of cases closed there is 5.160, according to the most recent information I have. So you see that this is an bit of a -- there is a bit of a discrepancy between those numbers, or difference between those numbers, let's say, that relates to the conditions that I've just explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: After having received this detailed explanation, I think it's now the right time for the second break. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Dr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, in response to General Tolimir's question in particular concerning the independent expert review, at page 50, I think it's lines 1 through 5, you made a reference to one of the factors that influenced the length of -- length of time in which to make an identification was a back-log of DNA. Do you recall giving an answer along those lines to one of General Tolimir's questions?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I just wanted to find out, at the moment, can you tell us approximately how large a back-log, if any, of bone samples remains to be tested?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presently we don't have a large back-log of samples waiting in queue for DNA. There remains in mortuaries many cases that need to be examined and sampled for DNA, or re-examined. Very often one result will provide information that will require additional tests to be made. So there is a continuing, ongoing DNA testing programme. And also there are remains that need to be found in the graves and exhumed, and those will also be tested.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned at some point in your cross-examination - I don't have the exact reference there - but you made some reference to certain information that is confidential with respect to the raw DNA data. Do you recall -- do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what specifically about raw DNA data would require the ICMP to keep that information confidential?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, DNA profiles are considered to be sensitive, private information. They're unique identifiers of the individual. So the raw DNA data, for example, the electropherogram data or the list of numbers that represent that, that we refer to as a DNA profile, is -- is generally considered to be data that should be protected. Moreover, and of more importance to us at the ICMP, we're dealing with families that have been traumatised and had members of their families murdered for -- for who they are. And they have very real concerns for their security and how their personal data is used. Our intent is to be able to return their loved ones to them. And we don't want them to be dissuaded from participating in this process, which can be considered a basic human right to know the fate of your loved ones, by additional concerns relighted to whether or not the -- who they believe to be the perpetrator of these deeds is going to have access to their genetic information. Whether or not their genetic information, if divulged to a third party, will wind up in some other database that is used to identify them. All these kind of concerns. So it -- it's absolutely essentially, for the role that we play, that the families have the greatest degree of comfort possible with regard to the security of their genetic data. And that's the basis of our protection policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you were required -- now, I understand that you've changed -- there was some change to the consent forms that were used in order to obtain, as it were, blood samples from donors, I think you indicated, in around 2007; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I indicated. But I have to emphasis: I'm not positive when that change came into effect. I believe it is documented in previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I would assume that there were a number of samples that were taken in advance of this change, probably several thousand. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, a great majority of the samples were obtained prior to that change.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the provision of those samples, if you were required to produce them without obtaining the consent of the family members, if you were inquired by court order or by some other means, can you tell us what impact that would have on the ICMP's efforts in Bosnia, or it's outreach programmes, and the ability to carry on the operation of identifying victims?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be essentially a mission destroying violation of the trust that has been established between the ICMP and the families, and, basically, I think, an end to our ability to do the type of work that we do, for the families to feel that their information can be -- can be obtained from us against the agreements that we've made with the families.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I wanted to show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could not broadcast this. And I think it has now a P number. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a -- I believe what we identified as case file on -- provided by the ICMP, concerning Bisina 01 Sekovici, and I think it's body number 40, that we looked at earlier. And a lot of reference has been made to electropherograms and the raw data during your cross-examination. What I wanted to show you was page 7, I think, of this document.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should be under --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The next page --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should not be publicly disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's right. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, nothing of that will be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, do you recognise what we have on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This is an electropherogram printout.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if you could just, in the simplest of terms, briefly explain what it shows.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's an indication of the alleles, which vary much in the -- which are variable in the population, that are present in this individual at 15 different chromosomal loci, plus an additional locus that indicates the sex of the individual, and that's the two peaks on the third panel that's marked X and Y. The rest of them are nuclear STR markers. And the numbers that you see listed underneath the peaks are the allelic values associated with the particular locus. As you look at this, you'll observe that they -- the peaks appear in pairs often. And those would be, in one instance, the maternal contribution and in the other instance the paternal contribution of an allele to that individual's genetic profile. Sometimes at a locus there's only one peak and that means that the individual inherited the same sized allele from both his mother and father and therefore you only have one peek at a locus instead of two even though they do have two copies of that same one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I make a suggestion. Can the witness mark the points he's referring to as he is speaking, because as we look at the image now, it's not quite clear which portion of the electropherogram is being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a very fair suggestion. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the Court Usher's assistance, the witness may do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that will be easier for us. So we have on here a series of peaks that represent alleles. So this would be one pair of alleles at a particular locus. So we see a peak associated with something that is sized as 15 and something that is sized as 16. And one of those two peaks, one of those two alleles, would have been inherited from the mother and the other allele would have been inherited from the father. So there's a series of these loci; there's 15 of them represented. Here's one where we see only a single peak at that locus, and in that case the individual inherited a 12 allele from both his mother and his father and that's why there's only a single peak there. I mentioned, about a locus, that indicates the sex of an individual. That would be this one. And it's labelled X and Y. And that has no information except whether the individual is a male or a female. If the individual is a female, there will be one peek labelled X. If it's a male, there'll be two peaks; one labelled X, the other labelled Y.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this marked exhibit, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And in combination with the transcript, I think it's clear what these circles depict. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1941, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, with respect to a match that is found or declared by the ICMP in accordance with the minimum threshold value for surety, the information that is found on the electropherograms, is that reflected on the match report?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These allelic values, once reviewed, are listed on the DNA match report just by virtue of the -- the numbers associated with these peaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are these values, as derived from the electropherograms, listed on each match report, for example, in the list that we've tendered here into evidence where you've indicated some 6.441 matches were found?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is a case file for each of these matches generated by the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the form that we would submit for review such as would be requested in the Bisina case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you mean to distinguish that from an electronic -- is it kept in an electronic form as opposed to a hard-copy form?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Out data is very carefully archived, both electronically and in hard copy, but is not maintained in separate case files. So to bring this information together for a single case requires substantial effort of collation, printing out, obtaining, checking, reviewing that everything that's in there that should be in there is in there. It's a very laborious process even for a single case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just roughly speaking, in order to produce these case files as the -- as the one we have in front of us, are they roughly the size of the file that we have in front of us? Here we have a file that's well over a hundred pages in hard copy. But are they generally of that size, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes. A hundred would seem large to me. But on the order of 50-some-odd pages, I would imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the record, the one we have here is about 131 pages.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a single case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: From a single case. All right. I'm finished with this exhibit. I'd like to ask you just a couple of other questions, if I may. You were asked about the independent expert review, on cross-examination, and I wanted to ask you a few questions arising from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's marked as D170. If we could have that in e-court, please, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First I just wanted to focus you on the composition of the panel. You indicated, I think, on cross-examination that these were noted experts in the field of DNA analysis. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very fair to say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about each of the individuals that comprise this panel?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite briefly, we have four individuals; two from the United States and two from Europe. Dr. Ingo Bastisch is the head of the Human DNA Laboratory for the Federal Criminal Police of Germany. And he is also the chairman of the DNA group of the European Network of Forensic Science Institutes. Dr. Cecelia Crouse is the chief scientific officer of the West Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, which is a highly technologically-advanced criminalistics laboratory in the United States, and she plays a very important role in the national scientific working group on DNA analysis methods in the United States. Professor Niels Morling is the director of the Department of Forensic Medicine at the University of Copenhagen and operates a very large and technology-advanced laboratory and moreover is president of the International Society on Forensic Genetics, the most prominent professional organisation relating to DNA typing in human identity. And then lastly is Dr. Mechthild Prinz, the director of forensic biology from the New York City office of the Chief Medical Examiner. And her laboratory system was involved in the World Trade Centre identifications, involving thousands of DNA tests of a similar nature to that which is performed at the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks for that. I'm just going ask you to slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to take you to some sections in the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go to page 12. Yes, that's right. And just under item number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: About midway through, the report talks about an intense and comprehensive review of each of the 1.582 DNA profiles. These are the profiles I think you eluded to in your cross-examination that were revisited.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It then reads that: "It was obvious to the expert review panel that a good-faith effort has been made by the ICMP to provide a complete accounting of the status of each of the 1.582 unmatched profiles as evidenced by the inordinate amount of research and analysis conducted by the Sarajevo DNA laboratory staff." Now, in respect of identifying 16 matches I think you referred to, was it necessary to either redo tests or reinterpret data in order to find those matches?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a quite extensive process of review, in many instances retesting, in many instances re-extraction, of DNA samples.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to take you to another section, and this will be on page -- the next page actually, page 13. And in the middle of the page, it reads that: "Due to the diligence of the forensic sciences director's initiative to conduct a quality check of the unmatched DNA profiles from 2001 to 2004, sample 9100507 was definitively matched to the Palic family reference samples." This is what you specifically addressed during your cross-examination. What I wanted to ask you was: In relation to the unfortunate circumstances resulting from a clerical error that resulted in the failure to match this sample, can you tell us, is it possible for such an error to produce a -- an erroneous match to an individual rather than result in the failure to match an individual?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- it's not the case that the type of error that was seen here would in any remote conception be expected to produce a false match. What these kind of errors, and almost any error in -- in a DNA-typing process, will do is to cause that DNA profile not to match properly. What -- what sporadic mistakes, large-scale mistakes, what have you, what they would do is -- what they would not do is transform one DNA profile into a matchable DNA profile of another individual. In other words, the types of errors that were investigated here are simply not expected to have affected any of the matches that we have made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more about why that's the case.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the genetic systems that we study, there are on the order of one hundred trillion trillion combinations that can be generated. So it's a number beyond astronomical conception. And when you're dealing in a universe, let's say, a pool of missing persons, that's several tens of thousands, the real genetic profiles are exceptionally rare compared to the genetic profiles that have never existed, the possible genetic profiles that have never existed. So if you make a random change in an individual's genetic profile, it's not going to -- it's not going to change it into another genetic profile relevant to that event. By astronomical odds it's going to change it into some other genetic profile that simply won't match anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me take you to another section of the report. And we'll go to page 24. Actually, we should start on page 23; I'm sorry. At the bottom of the page, we can see a summary. And it reads that: "Through the work in the Balkans and in disaster victim identification in other parts of the world, the ICMP has documented that the ICMP is obviously capable of working under difficult political and societal conditions and at the same time is able to apply technical and ethical standards at a high international level and reliably identify missing persons." It then goes on to talk about the accreditation according to the ISO 17025 standard. Prior to the accreditation by the accrediting committee -- first of all, could you tell us, the accrediting agency, who that is or what that is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a highly respected German accreditation agency with the abbreviations DAKKS. And I won't attempt to pronounce that in the German language.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the standard -- the ISO 17025 standard, can you describe for us, just in very brief terms, what that is?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a -- it's the most widely respected standard for accreditation relating to scientific and methodological processes where your laboratory is -- has a quality-management system that underlies all aspects of the work so that validated procedures are always used, and that you have standard operating procedures that indicate precisely what you do, and you have an ongoing series of audits that indicate that you do do what you should do, and a -- a mechanism for continual improvement and continual both self-monitoring and external audits by the accreditation body.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Prior to the accreditation that was obtained by the ICMP in 2007 I think you said it was, were there any fundamental substantive changes to the DNA testing procedure protocols or methodology from the period of time prior to that date?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obtaining accreditation did not map on to any substantive change as to the scientific procedures conducted at the ICMP. Was -- the largest change would have been associated with the degree of formal registration of documentation of procedures. But those actual procedures themselves were carried out virtually the same way, before and after.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if I could just take you to page 26 of the report and the second paragraph on the page, in the middle, it reads: "The number of new identifications" -- referring, I believe, to the 16 of the 1582 --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could clarify, briefly. At the time that this report was written, we hadn't conducted all the final follow-up experimentation and had only discovered at that time nine new identifications. The number today, having completed the exercise, is 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. It reads that: "The number of new identifications was also very low compared to the total number of identifications. These facts are in line with the impression of the expert review panel, that DNA and matching at the ICMP from inception was of high quality." Do you do anything fundamentally different in terms of testing procedures now than at the time that this review was carried out and at the time that the original testing was done prior to the review?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, the basic scientific methodology is the same. But we have an absolute commitment to continuing improvement. And through the action of our quality management system, we continually try to identify ways in which we can rule out the chances for human error. So, yes. And, in fact, throughout the entire period we've implemented continuing processes such as, now, independent witness checks. Where any time there's a transfer of samples at a key step from one vessel to another or one rack to another, we have independent observers to watch that process to help minimise the potential for human error in such -- in such a transfer. So it's those kind of things that have continued to be improved. Whenever possible, also, continually we've changed from any time that you would manually enter data to have that be an electronic transfer of data to the maximum extent possible. So for a large number of reasons, the events that gave rise to the unfortunate delay in the identification of Colonel Palic simply would not and could not happen today, for example. And many of those changes were made years ago, not just in response to having identified this problem with Colonel Palic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the context of the identification of Colonel Palic's remains, did the ICMP go back to and re-extract or re-test Avdo Palic's remains?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By that stage in the process, we were certainly going to investigate the issue to the maximum extent possible, so we obtained new samples from those skeletal remains cases, applied our current newer extraction methodology, and completely duplicated the results we had -- had previously obtained. I'll remind you that, in fact, the DNA profile we obtained from the Palic -- Colonel Palic's remains in the first instance was correct; it was simply incorrectly entered into the database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, it would be helpful only to use one microphone, because if you're using all the time two microphones, it -- this -- it makes your voice lower, surprisingly. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't realize they were both on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just like to ask both the Prosecutor and the expert to slow down a little bit because the transcript is far ahead of the interpretation that we're receiving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. It is an ongoing problem. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You were asked a question by General Tolimir - I think it would have been on page 59 of the transcript today - about whether the DNA identification was essentially a preliminary -- preliminary step in the ultimate identification of an individual as dead. Do you remember the question and an answer around -- concerning that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I wanted to ask: In terms of the work that the ICMP does, when you find that there's a distinct profile that you obtained from a -- an extracted bone, exhumed bone, is a profile synonymous with identifying an individual, not necessarily by name, but an -- a discrete person?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The types of profiles that we deal with, barring identical twins, can be expected to be unique to an individual within any bound of reasonable human experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So to the extent that the list of matches that was provided by the ICMP to the Office of the Prosecutor sets out some 6.441 identified individuals, it is fair to say that there are at least that many discrete DNA profiles to be found in that list?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And to the extent that these profiles came from Srebrenica-related graves, or the events concerning Srebrenica, would it be a fair inference to draw that they represent victims concerning the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the information we have received and our overall understanding of the nature of the event and our data, it's my opinion that these are victims of the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Having had an opportunity to oversee the process of DNA identification at the ICMP since 2006, can you state that the results of the DNA testing by the ICMP are, to a reasonable degree of scientific certainty, reliable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before the question will be answered, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise, but the Prosecutor is asking the expert's opinion. Is this an expert opinion that is presented in his report, or is it just his opinion? Since it's in contradiction with page 61 of the report where he said he doesn't have full control of the samples provided to him by the state commission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think that is pretty much addressed in the list itself. The list that was tendered is a list of DNA matching reports concerning Srebrenica-related individuals. So I think the question is a fair one, given that it was the witness's organisation that provided the OTP with that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was: Can you state the results -- that the results of the DNA testing by the ICMP are, to a reasonable degree -- scientific certainty, reliable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is absolutely my belief, based on extensive experience in this field and detailed knowledge of the ICMP's procedures, that our DNA match reports are wholly reliable. And although they are intended to be used in concert with all forensic evidence in a case, the ICMP considers that they are properly strong stand-alone in such cases where there would be no additional information. So the ICMP believes that this is exceptionally strong evidence of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no further questions on redirect examination. Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just need a number of clarifications. I'm trying to locate the page just so that I've got you correctly quoted. I think it's somewhere on page 68, lines 13 to 22, towards the end you -- correct me if I'm wrong or I'm quoting you wrongly, but you were recorded as having said: "... for the families to feel that their information can be obtained from us against their agreements that we have made with the families," you were talking about this in the context of the confidential lists? Have I quoted you right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you have, ma'am, and I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So this is my question: What sort of agreements does the ICMP have with the families with regard to this particular information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it relates to language on the consent form that indicates that their sample -- in providing their sample, we guarantee to them they'll be used only for the purposes of identification of their loved ones. And, moreover, we know from extensive interactions with the families that our sense of that has been communicated to them and is shared in their understanding that what they mean -- what we mean by that is that it will be used in order to return their loved one to them, as opposed, specifically, to being disclosed with regard to criminal proceedings such as this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question. It's with regard to the review panel. Who commissioned this review panel?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an initiative taken by the directors of the ICMP of whom I am one. So it was something that we felt was beneficial to all stakeholders involved, including ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: And then in the same, I think, 59, page 59, lines 6 to 8, you say: "It is not one of our absolute ... priorities because we think that there is very little risk that this system is causing any problems." So you say, in one breath, it's of no value?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, I wouldn't say that we consider it to be of no value. In fact, we are pursuing it. With regard to quality management in forensic laboratories, one of the most critical components to a continuing improvement is to identify those areas where there's the greatest risk. So in the laboratory, for example, eliminating human manipulations or eliminating the chances of human error is one of the very highest priorities you can have. We feel that through internal testing and our own internal design processes and internal validation studies that the forensic data management system that we have operates very, very strongly. We have absolute confidential -- well, absolute is not a word that should ever be used because it implies nothing could ever go wrong, and that's simply not a realistic situation. But we have a very, very high degree of confidence in the way that that system operates. So it will be beneficial if we can get a third party to come in and -- and validate, independently, the code. But, honestly, my feeling is it's not a -- an extremely important thing to do from the -- for the chances of preventing us from actually having problems. I'll mention, also, that it's a bit of a complex process to have software externally validated. And one of the reasons it's gone a little bit more slowly is we want to make sure that the process actually gives us what we want and need, in other words, takes an appropriate look at the system in a way that truly is valuable. And a second component that we're dealing with is it's actually a rather expensive undertaking and it relates to us requiring additional funds to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. But one last more question, Mr. Parsons, for you. I think it's page 25, lines 4 to 5. Please correct me if my -- I'm quoting you wrongly. You've said, in those lines: "I'm unaware of any other systematic use of nominal data in the manner that we are discussing it here." Do I understand you then to mean that nominal data has not been used anywhere else other than in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for drawing my attention to that. I would like to qualify that statement a little bit, with an emphasis on what I'm aware of. I will not -- I'm not a position to assert that it's never been used. I just don't know of any situations where it has been used or where I would guess, where I would predict, that it has been used in such a manner, so extensively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Have you used it yourself anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, ma'am. But it's possible that in the recording of the data that similar such things have been used in some instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're so welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes, now, your examination, Dr. Parsons. Thank you very much that you were able to come to The Hague again and provide us with your expertise. Now you are free to return to your normal activities. You are released. And it is now in your hands and it is your decision if you are able to meet with the Defence. That could help to clarify some matters and assist them to -- to prepare the Defence case. I would like to thank all those who are patient with us. We are over time a bit. I am looking forward to a fruitful week next week. We managed to finish with the scheduled witnesses this week, and I'm looking - and I refer to the comment of Mr. Gajic this morning - I'm looking forward to a fruitful, successful, and cooperation in the second year of this trial, which will commence next week. We adjourn and resume Monday in the afternoon, 2.15, in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of February, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.51 p.m.,
